units.title: Network layers, addressing, routing and DNS
outcomes: Use the OSI 7-layer and TCP/IP 4-layer models to place a failure at the right layer, and state where each model misleads.
Trace a DNS lookup from stub resolver through root, TLD and authoritative server, and apply the TTL expiry rule.
Read a host routing-table entry and predict the next hop with longest-prefix match.
units.why: Every later diagnosis in this section starts by asking which layer broke. Layers do not exist on the wire; they are a debugging vocabulary, and DNS plus routing are the two lookups every connection performs first.

next.note: Move one layer up to transport behavior on the path you can now address.
See what TLS and HTTP add above the addressed transport path.

study.title: The OSI 7-layer model
study.locator: The Seven Layers at a Glance; Encapsulation Across the Stack; Using OSI to Diagnose a Failure; Where the Model Has Limits

study.title: The TCP/IP 4-layer model
study.locator: The Four Layers; Mapping TCP/IP to OSI; A Complete Request in TCP/IP Terms; Boundaries in Modern Protocols

study.locator: Chapter 4, The Layered Network Model (Sections 4.3 and 4.4); Chapter 18, IP Routing (Sections 18.2 to 18.5)

study.title: DNS hierarchy and debugging
study.locator: Domains and Zones Are Different; Following the Chain of Authority; Practical Implications for Engineers; then Debugging DNS with dig and nslookup: The Basic dig Command, Walk the Delegation with +trace, Diagnose Cache and TTL Behavior
study.depth: Use https://algomaster.io/learn/computer-networks/debugging-dns for the dig sections; skip DNSSEC detail.

focus: OSI layers are an explanatory model. The wire carries frames, packets and segments; nothing is tagged with a layer number.
DNS resolution is a chain of referrals with per-record TTLs. A cached answer is valid while now is earlier than stored time plus TTL; reading it does not refresh it.
Routing is longest-prefix match on the destination, per packet, per hop. The default route is only the shortest prefix that matches.
Sending adds transport, internet and link headers around application data in that order; receiving strips them in reverse.
units.reproduce: Run dig +short example.com twice and compare the answer sets. Then closed-book, write the cold-lookup chain (stub to recursive to root to TLD to authoritative) and evaluate the TTL rule on store(api.example, 192.0.2.10, TTL 10, t=100): resolve at t=109 hits, at t=110 misses.
traps: Treating OSI as seven things a packet passes through in code. Implementations merge and skip layers; TLS, for example, sits between transport use and the application.
Reading a DNS TTL as a freshness guarantee. It bounds staleness; an authoritative change still waits out the TTL at every cache.
Inferring network meaning from dotted quads or old class letters. Only the prefix length defines the network part.

selfTest.q: A record stored at t=100 with TTL 10 is resolved at t=110. Hit or miss, and why?
selfTest.a: Miss. It is valid only while \(now < 100 + 10\), and resolving does not refresh the expiry.

selfTest.q: Entries cover 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.2.0/24. Which carries a packet for 10.1.2.9?
selfTest.a: 10.1.2.0/24. Longest-prefix match wins; the /24 is more specific than the /8.

selfTest.q: Why can two applications on one host share one IP address without conflict?
selfTest.a: The transport port number separates them. The IP address names the host; the port names the socket endpoint.

selfTest.q: A capture shows HTTP inside TLS inside TCP inside IPv4 inside Ethernet. Which layering claim does this support?
selfTest.a: Encapsulation order only. It shows headers wrapped around data; it does not prove a seven-layer implementation.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Implement a DNS TTL Cache
practice.locator: store and resolve with TTL expiry (\(now < t + d\)), case-insensitive names, cached NXDOMAIN
practice.note: Do not refresh expiry on resolve; the 109-hit 110-miss boundary in Reproduce is the first case to pass.

units.stopWhen: You place a refused connection, an NXDOMAIN and a wrong route at the right layer on the first guess, and your TTL cache passes the 109-hit 110-miss boundary.

fit.note: Beej layering and routing chapters plus the AlgoMaster OSI, TCP/IP and DNS lessons cover both topics, and the TTL-cache problem gives named practice.

units.title: TCP and UDP transport behavior
outcomes: Explain the TCP service contract: reliable ordered duplicate-suppressed byte stream, setup cost, and what an ACK does not promise.
Contrast UDP datagrams with TCP streams and choose between them from loss, ordering and latency needs.
Read zero-window, retransmission and congestion evidence in a capture and name the limiting mechanism.
units.why: Sockets expose streams, not messages. Misreading TCP as a message protocol causes every framing bug in the next unit, and confusing flow control with congestion control misdirects tuning.

next.note: Build message framing on top of the byte stream.
Turn setup cost and window stalls into pool and latency policy.

study.depth: Follow the phase method and the window evidence. The audit-pipe root cause is one example of host correlation, not a pattern to memorize.

study.title: Congestion control vocabulary (optional topic)
study.locator: Flow Control and Congestion Control Solve Different Problems; Slow Start; Congestion Avoidance and AIMD
study.depth: Vocabulary only for the optional topic. No measurement required; stop before the variant comparison.

focus: TCP numbers bytes, not messages. The ACK advances over the contiguous prefix; a gap stalls acknowledgment even when later bytes arrived.
An ACK means the peer kernel holds the bytes. It does not mean the application read or acted on them.
Flow control (receiver window) and congestion control (sender network estimate) are independent limits; the sender obeys the smaller.
UDP preserves message boundaries and promises nothing else. Loss, duplication and reordering are normal and must be handled above it.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the three handshake messages with initial sequence numbers (client \(c\), server \(s\)) and the ACK numbers \(c+1\) and \(s+1\). Then, on loopback with CPython 3.14.4, run a server thread that accepts and closes, and time 100 create_connection plus close calls after 10 warm-up ones; then time 200 round trips of a 4-byte length-prefixed echo (TCP_NODELAY, 20 warm-up) at 64 bytes and 64 KiB. Pinned to two performance cores with taskset -c 2,4 on an i9-12900K with Linux 7.0, three runs gave connect plus close medians of 12 to 16 us, a 64 B echo p50 of about 9 us and a 64 KiB p50 of about 29 us; unpinned runs that landed on efficiency cores were up to about twice as slow. Record yours with the same setup and say which cores ran it.
traps: Calling a retransmission proof of packet loss. Delayed ACKs, reordering and spurious timeouts cause retransmissions on healthy paths.
Expecting close to deliver pending application work. A graceful FIN ends the byte stream; it says nothing about processed requests.
Treating UDP as TCP without acknowledgments. Without sequence numbers and reassembly above it, duplicates and reordering reach the application.

selfTest.q: Segments \([0,3)\) and \([5,7)\) arrived. Which byte does the receiver ACK next?
selfTest.a: Byte 3. The ACK covers only the contiguous prefix from 0; bytes 5 and 6 wait behind the gap at 3 and 4.

selfTest.q: The client advertised a zero window for five seconds, then the transfer resumed with no retransmissions. Where was the stall?
selfTest.a: At the receiving endpoint: its buffer stayed full because the application stopped reading. The network and server were waiting on window updates.

selfTest.q: Why does a fresh TCP connection cost at least one round trip before data flows?
selfTest.a: SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK must synchronize sequence numbers and open state on both ends; data normally starts after the exchange.

selfTest.q: Two identical datagrams arrive over UDP. Did the network duplicate one, or did the sender retransmit?
selfTest.a: UDP alone cannot tell. Both look identical; only an application sequence number distinguishes a duplicate from a retry.

practice.note: The gap example ([[0,3],[5,2]] returns 3) is the ACK rule in code; overlapping intervals must not double-count.

units.stopWhen: You classify a stall as receiver-window, loss-recovery or endpoint silence from window and ACK evidence, and your reassembler returns 3 and 5 on the two worked examples.

fit.note: The AlgoMaster transport lessons plus Beej TCP/UDP chapters cover all three topics at explain and measure depth, with the pcap lab and the reassembler problem as practice.

study.title: Minimal HTTP exchange vocabulary
study.locator: Chapter 5, Section 5.3 (HTTP Summary) only
study.depth: Read Section 5.3 only. The chapter 5 client and server projects belong to the sockets and HTTP practice in later units.

focus: ServerHello proves nothing about identity. Authentication is the certificate chain plus CertificateVerify plus Finished checked against the handshake transcript.
TLS 1.3 with ephemeral keys gives forward secrecy: a stolen long-term key does not decrypt recorded sessions.
ALPN negotiates the application protocol inside TLS. A compatible handshake can still fail with no_application_protocol.

The HTTP versions share semantics and differ on the wire: ordered text messages, multiplexed streams over one TCP connection, streams over QUIC. HTTP/2 removes HTTP-level head-of-line blocking but keeps TCP's; HTTP/3 keeps it only within one stream.
units.reproduce: Run curl -w with time_namelookup, time_connect, time_appconnect, time_starttransfer and http_version against https://example.com/ three times, and note your curl and TLS library versions and whether DNS was warm. State which interval is DNS, which is TCP, which adds TLS, and why three requests from one place cannot characterize the service.
traps: Believing the certificate encrypts the data. Ephemeral key exchange protects records; the certificate only authenticates.
Expecting TLS to hide everything. Server name, record sizes and timing stay visible; that is why session key logs are secrets.
Calling HTTP/3 faster by definition. It removes TCP head-of-line blocking and can resume faster; path, server and loss still decide.

selfTest.q: A capture shows ClientHello, ServerHello, then opaque records. Can you read the HTTP path?
selfTest.a: No. Everything after ServerHello is encrypted in TLS 1.3. Endpoints, ports, timing and sizes remain; the path needs endpoint logs or key material.

selfTest.q: time_appconnect minus time_connect is 25 ms. What does that interval contain?
selfTest.a: Roughly the TLS handshake after TCP connected: certificate, key exchange and Finished plus their round trips. It is cumulative and approximate.

selfTest.q: Which head-of-line blocking does HTTP/2 keep?
selfTest.a: TCP-level blocking. One lost TCP segment stalls every multiplexed stream on that connection; HTTP/3 moves recovery to per-stream QUIC.

selfTest.q: The server presents a valid certificate for another hostname. Does the handshake succeed?
selfTest.a: No for a correct client. Every signature can verify, but the name check fails, so the client aborts with a certificate alert instead of sending application data.

study.title: A production-shaped echo protocol
study.locator: The Persistent Echo Protocol (4-byte big-endian length prefix, 64 KiB limit); Concurrency Boundaries; Admission Before Task Creation
study.depth: Adopt the length prefix, size limit and 30-second frame deadline. Leave the Java port and the load client for the latency unit.

focus: Every recv can return one byte, one frame, several frames, or anything between. The parser keeps explicit state: bytes still needed for the header, then bytes still needed for the payload.
sendall is a loop, not a guarantee. A raw send can write fewer bytes; the remainder must be retried, not dropped.
Limits come before parsing: check the declared length against the maximum before allocating or reading the payload.
A version or length violation is a protocol error. Reply if the protocol allows, then close. Never resynchronize by scanning payload bytes for a magic value.
units.reproduce: With CPython 3.14.4 on loopback, send two frames of a 4-byte length prefix plus 10 bytes back-to-back (28 wire bytes), wait until both sends have landed, then read with recv(5): exactly 6 calls return all bytes. Repeat with one recv(4096): a single call returns all 28 bytes, both frames coalesced. Then feed your framer the same bytes split at every offset and check it yields the same two messages each time.
traps: Assuming one send equals one recv. Coalescing and splitting are normal; the 28-byte two-frame burst routinely arrives in one recv on loopback.
Growing the buffer from the declared length without a cap. A corrupt 4 GB prefix becomes a memory-exhaustion attack; validate first.
Treating a clean FIN mid-frame as a complete message. A peer that began a frame and closed sent a truncated message: a protocol error, not a short message.

selfTest.q: recv(5) returned 3 bytes of a 4-byte header, then the next recv returns 0 bytes. What happened and what does the framer do?
selfTest.a: The peer closed mid-frame. The framer reports a truncation protocol error; the 3 bytes are not a message.

selfTest.q: The length prefix says 100 bytes but only 60 arrived and there was no FIN. What does the framer do?
selfTest.a: It waits with the receive deadline running. A partial payload is state (40 bytes still needed), not an error, until the deadline or close.

selfTest.q: Why check the length against 64 KiB before reading the payload?
selfTest.a: To bound allocation and read work from untrusted bytes. Reading first lets a bogus prefix force a huge allocation.

selfTest.q: Two frames arrive in one recv. Does the application need two reads?
selfTest.a: No. The framer consumes both from the buffered bytes and delivers two messages; read count and message count are unrelated.

study.title: Traceparent and tracestate
study.locator: Section 3.2 (traceparent format and examples); Sections 3.4 to 3.5 (legal mutations when forwarding)

focus: Wire identity is the field number, not the name. In the binary encoding, renaming tag 2 is compatible; changing 2 to 4 deletes a field and creates another. JSON mappings use names, so a rename breaks them.
proto3 scalars conflate absent with default. Use optional, oneof or message fields when the distinction changes behavior.
HTTP 200 with a nonzero grpc-status is an RPC failure. Monitors that check only HTTP status report success while every call fails.
Forwarding a trace means sending traceparent with a new parent-id and preserving tracestate order; a hop that regenerates the trace-id splits the trace.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, parse 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01 into version 00, 16-byte trace-id, 8-byte parent-id and sampled flag, and state the legal forwarding mutations (new parent-id, optional sampled change, restart, downgrade). Then add a request-id field to your framed protocol and show it echoed unchanged in the response.
traps: Reusing a deleted field number for a new type. Old binaries parse the new bytes as the old type; use a fresh number.
Hiding errors inside OK responses. Clients, retry policies and metrics can only reason about errors carried in status.
Putting secrets or high-cardinality values into trace context. traceparent and tracestate propagate to every downstream service, and the spec forbids personally identifying data there.

selfTest.q: Field 2 changes from string to int32 with the same number. Wire-compatible?
selfTest.a: No. A string travels length-delimited and an int32 as a varint, so old readers cannot decode it as their string; most runtimes keep it as an unknown field and the value is lost to them. Add a new field number instead.

selfTest.q: A proxy returns HTTP 200 for an RPC that failed with grpc-status 14. What should the dashboard show?
selfTest.a: An RPC failure with UNAVAILABLE. Transport success and RPC outcome are separate channels.

selfTest.q: A service forwards traceparent byte-identical and appends its tracestate entry. Correct?
selfTest.a: No. It must set parent-id to its own current operation ID; byte-identical forwarding claims the downstream work is the same span. New tracestate entries go first, not last.

selfTest.q: Why must the server application stop its own work when gRPC signals cancellation for deadline?
selfTest.a: The runtime only signals; spawned database calls and child RPCs keep running and consuming resources until the application stops them.

study.title: gRPC deadlines, cancellation and retries
study.locator: Deadlines, Cancellation, and Retries: realistic deadlines, application-owned cancellation, retry only safe-to-repeat operations

focus: Every timeout hides three possible server states: never saw it, executed and failed to reply, executed and reply lost. Retry design starts by listing all three.
Deadlines are absolute points in time; timeouts are durations. Propagate the remaining time, never a fresh full timeout, or downstream work outlives the caller.
A retry budget bounds attempts per operation and per fleet. Unbounded per-hop retries multiply across layers into a retry storm.
Idempotency keys need a durable state machine (received, in-progress, completed) with atomic transitions; memory-only dedup forgets across restarts.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, propagate startTime 0 and client timeout 100 through processing times [10,20,5] with local bounds [80,100,10]: hop deadlines [90,90,45]. Then run the deterministic proxy on loopback (CPython 3.14.4): 200 ms injected delay with a 100 ms client deadline records a client timeout although the server processed the request; the duplicate proxy leaves a second frame waiting on the connection. Reference run on kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, i9-12900K confirmed both rows.
traps: Retrying on DEADLINE_EXCEEDED without an idempotency key. The first attempt may have completed; the retry repeats the side effect.
Resetting a full timeout at each hop. Three hops with fresh 2 s timeouts let downstream work run until about 6 s, 4 s after a 2 s caller has given up.
Treating at-most-once as safety. Never resending avoids duplicates but turns every lost reply into a user-visible failure; choose the semantics per operation.

selfTest.q: The client timeout fires at 100 ms; the server log shows the write committed at 150 ms. What does the client know?
selfTest.a: Nothing about the outcome. The timeout only proves the reply did not arrive in time; the effect may have happened, and only a keyed status check can resolve it.

selfTest.q: Two layers each retry up to 3 times on failure. What is the worst-case attempt count for one user request?
selfTest.a: Up to 16: the outer layer makes 1 initial attempt plus 3 retries, and each of the 4 can trigger up to 4 inner attempts. Layered retries multiply.

selfTest.q: Why does gRPC convert a deadline to a remaining-time timeout before forwarding?
selfTest.a: Server clocks may disagree. Sending a duration shields propagation from clock skew; sending an absolute timestamp does not.

selfTest.q: A duplicate arrives while the first attempt is still IN_PROGRESS. What does the state machine do?
selfTest.a: It never starts the effect a second time. It waits for the first attempt within its own deadline, returns a documented in-progress response, or returns an operation the client can poll; the stored result is replayed once it exists.

study.title: A latency decomposition worked example
study.locator: Turn the Stream into a Timeline; Inspect the Edges of the Gap
study.depth: Read as a decomposition method: phase table first, then edges of the dominant gap. You already studied its flow-control mechanism in the transport unit.

focus: Each direction closes independently. shutdown for writing sends FIN while the read side stays open; close with unread data still queued can reset the connection.
TIME-WAIT belongs to the active closer and lasts twice the maximum segment lifetime; a lingering CLOSE-WAIT means the application never closed, which is a leak, not a TCP quirk.
Pool size follows offered concurrency: arrival rate times hold time, plus headroom. Pool keys must include every security boundary (host, TLS identity, credentials), never just the IP.
One client number never decomposes itself. DNS, connect, TLS, queue, handler and dependency times come from different instruments; subtract only compatible timestamps.
units.reproduce: Derive the pool size closed-book: 600 requests/s times 50 ms mean hold gives 30 busy connections, so 20 cannot sustain the average and exactly 30 leaves no burst headroom. Then split one HTTPS request to https://example.com/ into DNS, connect, TLS and first-byte intervals with curl -w, three times, and report the numbers with your curl and TLS library versions and warm or cold DNS.
traps: Reusing a connection across hostnames that resolve to one IP. Certificates and authorization attach to names, not addresses.
Treating starttransfer minus appconnect as server time. It still includes request travel, queueing and first-byte return.
Draining by closing the listener only. In-flight requests, keep-alive connections and load-balancer caches need explicit propagation, a grace budget and a forced-stop step.

selfTest.q: ss shows many sockets in CLOSE-WAIT. Whose bug is it?
selfTest.a: The local application's. The peer closed its side; the local end never closed its socket, so the state persists.

selfTest.q: A pool holds 20 HTTP/1.1 connections at 600 requests/s with 50 ms holds. What happens?
selfTest.a: Waiters accumulate without bound. The pool sustains about 400 requests/s; the excess queues, and latency and memory grow.

selfTest.q: Why must a pool discard a connection that received Connection: close?
selfTest.a: The server will not accept another exchange on it. Lending it out guarantees the next borrower fails.

selfTest.q: A pcap shows a 5 s gap with zero-window advertisements and no retransmissions. Which latency component grew?
selfTest.a: None of the network components. An endpoint stall at the receiver inflated total time; DNS, connect and TLS phases were already complete.

study.title: Failure modes and unknown outcomes
study.locator: A Network Call Has Several Failure Points; Timeouts Turn Unbounded Waiting into a Decision; Known Failure, Known Success, and Unknown Outcome

study.title: Observable overload and failure behavior
study.locator: Overload Behavior Is Observable; Failure Behavior; Common Failure Patterns
study.depth: Read for the failure-injection checklist; you already implemented the server contract in the sockets unit.

focus: Deterministic means seeded and scripted: same fault schedule, same interleaving, same verdict. Random chaos finds bugs; only replayable schedules prove fixes.
Inject above TCP when testing the protocol (duplicate frames, truncated writes, slow reads) and at the connection level when testing the path (delay, drop, restart).
Each fault has an expected client observation: delay past deadline gives timeout with unknown outcome; duplicate gives one effect under keys; drop gives disconnect with unknown outcome.
Restart is two faults at once: in-flight requests resolve as unknown, and post-restart state must reconcile pre-restart keys by policy.
units.reproduce: Run the three-case proxy matrix on loopback (CPython 3.14.4): 200 ms injected delay with a 100 ms client deadline records timeout; duplicate delivery leaves a second frame waiting on the connection; response drop records disconnect. Extend the script with a restart case and record all four rows with the fault parameters beside each verdict. Reference run on Linux x86-64 kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, i9-12900K confirmed the first three rows.
traps: Counting a passed clean-path test as fault coverage. Timeouts, duplicates and restarts exercise different code than the happy path.
Driving fault timing from wall-clock sleeps with tight deadlines. Slow machines flake; script explicit fault steps with generous margins.
Logging faults only at the injector. Verdicts need client observation, server state and the schedule in one record, or failures cannot be replayed.

selfTest.q: The delay fault fires but the client still reports success. Is the test wrong?
selfTest.a: Either the deadline exceeds the injected delay or the client has no deadline. A fault test must assert the client observation, not just run the injector.

selfTest.q: Why must the duplicate test read twice?
selfTest.a: The first read succeeds in both correct and buggy servers. Only the second read shows whether a duplicate arrived, and the effect log shows whether it executed twice.

selfTest.q: The server restarts between request receipt and response. What may the client conclude?
selfTest.a: Only that the outcome is unknown. The effect may or may not have committed; resolution needs a keyed status query after reconnect.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the full fault matrix (partial, coalesced, oversized, malformed, timeout, duplicate, disconnect, restart) against the versioned framed service, with replayable schedules and verdict records.
units.stopWhen: Your proxy replays a scripted fault schedule, every row records fault parameters with client observation and server state, and you can state the exact delivery guarantee in one sentence.

fit.note: The project fault matrix plus the failure-mode vocabulary cover the topic; integrated practice belongs to the section mini-project by checkpoint design.
